questions.question: What is meant by the Thermidorian Reaction. / [CO1, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by the Thermidorian Reaction - [K] / [CO1, CO5] - The Thermidorian
  • Reaction (July 1794) was the counter -revolutionary revolt within the French National
  • Convention that overthrew and executed Maximilien Robespierre, ending the Reign of Terror.
  • It marked a conservative turn in the French Revolution, lead ing to the dismantling of Jacobin
  • policies and the establishment of the Directory in 1795.

questions.question: Recall the Quadruple Alliance. / [CO1, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Recall the Quadruple Alliance - [K] / [CO1, CO5] - The Quadruple Alliance (1815) was a
  • coalition formed by Britain, Austria, Prussia, and Russia following Napoleon's defeat, aimed
  • at maintaining the balance of power established by the Congress of Vienna. It served as a
  • collective security mechanism to s uppress revolutionary movements and prevent French
  • aggression in Europe.

questions.question: Recall the significance of the 'Kingdom of Rome'. / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Recall the significance of the 'Kingdom of Rome' - [U] / [CO1, CO2] - The Kingdom of
  • Rome refers to the title given to Napoleon Bonaparte's son, Napoleon II, born in 1811,
  • symbolizing Napoleon's ambition to establish a hereditary imperial dynasty stretching across
  • Europe. Its significance lies in Napoleon's intention to legitimize his empire and secure a lasting
  • Bonapartist succession, though the kingdom never materialized as a real political entity after
  • his fall.

questions.question: What is meant by the Balkan Wars? / [CO1, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by the Balkan Wars? - [K] / [CO1, CO4] - The Balkan Wars (1912–1913)
  • were two successive conflicts in which the Balkan League (Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece, and
  • Montenegro) first defeated the Ottoman Empire to gain territorial independence, and then
  • fought among themselves over the division of tho se territories. These wars significantly
  • weakened the Ottoman presence in Europe and heightened nationalist tensions that directly
  • contributed to the outbreak of World War I.

questions.question: Pearl Harbour Attack. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Pearl Harbour Attack. - [K] / [CO1] - The Pearl Harbour Attack on December 7, 1941, was
  • a surprise military strike by the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service against the United States
  • naval base at Pearl Harbour, Hawaii, killing over 2,400 Americans and destroying numerous
  • battleships and aircraft. This attack directly prompted the United States to formally enter World
  • War II by declaring war on Japan the following day.

questions.question: What is meant by neoliberalism? / [CO3, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by neoliberalism? - [K] / [CO3, CO4] - Neoliberalism is an economic and
  • political ideology that advocates for free -market capitalism, deregulation, privatization,
  • reduction of government spending, and the liberalization of trade and investment. It rose to
  • global prominence in the 1970s –80s, particularly associated with the policies of Margaret
  • Thatcher in the UK and Ronald Reagan in the USA.

questions.question: What is meant by Foreign Direct Investment? / [CO3, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by Foreign Direct Investment? - [K] / [CO3, CO4] - Foreign Direct Investment
  • (FDI) refers to an investment made by a company or individual in one country into business
  • interests in another country, typically involving establishing business operations or acquiring
  • business assets such as ownership or con trolling interest in a foreign company. FDI is a key
  • feature of economic globalization and plays a significant role in the development of host
  • economies by transferring capital, technology, and expertise.

questions.question: Who was Jomo Kenyatta? / [CO1, CO2, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Who was Jomo Kenyatta? - [K] / [CO1, CO2, CO4] - Jomo Kenyatta was a Kenyan
  • nationalist leader who led Kenya's struggle for independence from British colonial rule and
  • became the country's first Prime Minister and subsequently its first President. He is regarded
  • as the founding father of modern Kenya and a prominent figure in African anti -colonial
  • movements.

questions.question: What is meant by Cold War? / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by Cold War? - [K] / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4] - The Cold War was a prolonged
  • period of geopolitical tension (1947–1991) between the United States and its Western allies on one
  • side and the Soviet Union and its Eastern bloc on the other, characterized by ideological rivalry
  • between capitalism and communism without direct large-scale military conflict between the two
  • superpowers. It manifested through proxy wars, nuclear arms races, space competition, and
  • political interventions across Asia, Africa, Latin America, and Europe

questions.question: What is meant by Ku Klux Clan? / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by Ku Klux Clan? - [K] / [CO1, CO2] - The Ku Klux Klan is a white
  • supremacist, far-right extremist organization founded in the United States in 1865 following the
  • Civil War, notorious for using terror, violence, and intimidation against African Americans, Jews,
  • immigrants, and other minority groups. The Klan experienced multiple waves of resurgence and
  • remains a symbol of racial hatred and domestic terrorism in American history.

questions.question: Examine the French and English imperialism in Asia and Africa. / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the French and English imperialism in Asia and Africa.- [U] / [CO1, CO2] - France
  • established a major presence in North Africa by capturing Algiers in 1830 and Tunisia in 1881,
  • while further extending control over Morocco, Ivory Coast, Dahomey, Gabon, and Eastern
  • Sudan, consolidating a vast African empire through military force and diplomatic negotiations.
  • Britain, driven by strategic and economic interests, bombarded Alexandria in 1882 to seize
  • Egypt and control the Suez Canal, and expanded fur ther into Nigeria, Kenya, Buganda,
  • Tanganyika, Rhodesia, and South Africa, using superior military technology and railroad
  • construction to consolidate its dominance. The West African Conference of Berlin (1884),
  • attended by fifteen nations, formalized the European scramble for Africa by establishing
  • ground rules for colonial acquisition, with Britain and France emerging as the dominant powers
  • dividing territories such as Togoland, Cameroon, and Sudan between themselves. Following
  • World War I, the mandate sy stem further reinforced Anglo -French imperial supremacy, with
  • France receiving Syria, Lebanon, and portions of Togoland and Cameroon, while Britain
  • gained Iraq, Palestine, Transjordan, and additional African territories, cementing their
  • combined imperial dominance across Asia and Africa.

questions.question: Observe the concept of imperialism discussed in the writings of Bukharin. / [CO1, CO3]

• Observe the concept of imperialism discussed in the writings of Bukharin. - [U] / [CO1,
  • CO3] Bukharin stated that 'Imperialism as the reproduction of capitalist competition on a large
  • scale'. His argument moves from imperialism as a policy and as an ideology, to imperialism as
  • a characteristic of the world economy at a particular stage of develop ment. Imperialist
  • annexation is only a case of the general capitalist tendency towards centralization of capital, a
  • case of its centralization at that maximum scale which corresponds to the competition of state
  • capitalist trusts.

questions.question: Critically analyse the working of the economic policy of War Communism in Soviet Russia. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Critically analyse the working of the economic policy of War Communism in Soviet Russia.
  • - [An] / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO5] – Economic policy prevailed in between 1917 and 1921
  • evolved out of the desperate measures taken to supply the battlefront with needed materials
  • and manpower. One feature of War Communism was the nationalization of land, banks, foreign
  • trade, and heavy in dustry. Another was the forcible requisitioning of surplus agricultural
  • produce needed to feed the soldiers and the city dwellers. The original plan was to compensate
  • the peasants with manufactured goods, but this proved impossible because almost all factories
  • were producing for the front. Industrial and agricultural production went down.

questions.question: Examine the antisemitic ideological propagation in the Nazi Germany. / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the antisemitic ideological propagation in the Nazi Germany.- [U] / [CO1, CO2]
  • – The Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of their citizenship, reducing them to second-class status
  • based on "impure blood" defined by their grandparents' religion, while "Racial Science" was
  • introduced into school curricula to institutionalize anti -Semitism across German society. In
  • November 1938, state-coordinated attacks destroyed 267 synagogues, killed at least 91 Jews,
  • and sent thousands to concentration camps in what was falsely presented as spontaneous public
  • violence, marking a dramatic escalation of persecution. Nazi policy progressively shifted from
  • expulsion to systematic extermination, with killing squads murdering entire Jewish
  • communities, gas chambers establis hed in dedicated death camps like Auschwitz, and over
  • 700,000 Jews killed at Treblinka alone within five months. The Holocaust culminated in the
  • murder of between 4 to 6 million European Jews

questions.question: Discuss the origin of the Great Depression of 1930s in USA. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the origin of the Great Depression of 1930s in USA. [U] / [CO3] - The
  • fundamental cause of the Great Depression was a sharp decline in consumer spending and
  • demand, which led to reduced production, while the American economic collapse was further
  • transmitted to the rest of the world through the gold standard. The war tim e benefits like
  • exporting of both grains and guns to Europe got arrested following the peace settlements. Stock
  • prices had risen fourfold between 1921 and 1929 to unjustifiable levels, and when minor events
  • triggered gradual price declines in October 1929, investor confidence collapsed, leading to the
  • infamous "Black Thursday" panic on October 24, 1929, when a record 12.9 million shares were
  • traded in a single day. The subsequent Great Crash saw US stock prices decline by 33 percent
  • between September and November 1929, dramatically reducing American aggregate demand
  • and triggering a cycle of liquidation that devastated the broader economy. Banking panics
  • compounded the crisis as depositors simultaneously withdrew savings, forcing banks to hastily
  • liquidate loans, causing even solvent banks to fail, ultimately culminating in the national bank
  • holiday declared by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on March 6, 1933.

questions.question: Analyse the significant characteristics of a dependent economy. / [CO2, CO3, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Analyse the significant characteristics of a dependent economy. - [U] / [CO2, CO3, CO4] -
  • Underdeveloped countries experience unsatisfactory economic growth as profits extracted by
  • core countries are repatriated rather than reinvested locally, while their export industries remain
  • heavily dependent on imported inputs, creating a cycle of stru ctural dependency. The income,
  • employment, and growth of underdeveloped economies are dictated not by local market
  • conditions but by international market prices, external demand fluctuations, and the investment
  • decisions of transnational corporations. Economic stability in underdeveloped nations is further
  • conditioned by volatile import prices, economic fluctuations abroad, shifting global tastes and
  • fashions, and the emergence of technologically created substitutes that undermine their export
  • competitiveness. Foreign capital, foreign technology, and foreign management dominate as the
  • principal economic actors, leaving underdeveloped economies with little autonomous co ntrol
  • over their own development trajectory.

questions.question: Examine the relevance of the UN organ Trusteeship Council in contemporary times. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the relevance of the UN organ Trusteeship Council in contemporary times. [E] /
  • [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4] - The Trusteeship Council was established in 1945 as one of the six
  • principal organs of the United Nations, with the primary mandate of supervising the
  • administration of trust territories and guiding them toward self-governance and independence.
  • The Council successfully fulfilled its original mandate when Palau, the last remaining trust
  • territory, achieved independence in 1994, after which the Cou ncil formally suspended its
  • operations on November 1, 1994, meeting only on an extraordinary basis when needed. In
  • contemporary times, the Trusteeship Council is widely regarded as largely redundant and
  • obsolete in its original form, as there are no remain ing trust territories under its supervision,
  • prompting ongoing debates within the UN regarding its reformation or complete abolition.
  • However, some scholars and UN reformers argue for its reinvention as a body overseeing
  • global commons such as the environment, deep seabed resources, and outer space, suggesting
  • a potential contemporary relevance if restructured to address modern challenge s of global
  • governance.

questions.question: Discuss the nature of the student movement in France in 1968. / [CO1, CO2, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the nature of the student movement in France in 1968. [U] / [CO1, CO2, CO4] -
  • The French student movement of 1968, known as "Mai 68," originated at the University of
  • Nanterre and spread to the Sorbonne in Paris, where students protested against authoritarian
  • university administration, outdated educational structures, and the cons ervative social values
  • of Gaullist France, drawing heavily from Marxist, anarchist, and existentialist ideologies to
  • challenge capitalism and American imperialism. The s tudent uprising rapidly transcended
  • academic grievances to catalyze a massive general strike involving nearly ten million French
  • workers, paralyzing the French economy and transforming a campus revolt into the largest
  • general strike in French history, brin ging the country to the brink of revolution. Though de
  • Gaulle's government survived by calling snap elections and winning a landslide victory, Mai
  • 68 left a profound cultural legacy, fundamentally reshaping French society by accelerating
  • social liberalizat ion, feminist movements, workers' rights, and the democratization of
  • education in the decades that followed.

questions.question: Discuss the Chinese nationalist revolution under Sun Yat-sen. / [CO1, CO2, CO5] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the Chinese nationalist revolution under Sun Yat-sen. [U] / [CO1, CO2, CO5] -
  • Sun Yat-sen, widely regarded as the father of modern China, founded the Tongmenghui
  • revolutionary alliance in 1905 and developed his ideological framework of the "Three
  • Principles of the People" — nationalism, democracy, and people's livelihood — as the
  • philosophical foundation for overthrowing the declining Qing dynasty and ending centuries of
  • imperial rule. The successful Xinhai Revolution of 1911 abolished the Qing dynasty and
  • established the Republic of China, with Sun Yat -sen briefly serving as its first provisional
  • president before being forced to yield power to the militarist Yuan Shikai, exposing the fragility
  • of the new republican order against entrenched warlo rd power. Sun Yat -sen subsequently
  • reorganized his nationalist movement into the Kuomintang (KMT) party in 1912, and with
  • Soviet assistance restructured it along Leninist lines in 1923, forging the First United Front
  • with the Chinese Communist Party to pur sue national unification, a legacy that continued to
  • shape Chinese political development long after his death in 1925.
  • [5x6 = 30]

questions.question: Illustrate the political process of the unification of German states to a nation. / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Illustrate the political process of the unification of German states to a nation. [U] / [CO1,
  • CO2] - Modern German nationalism emerged in the late 18th century, stimulated by the French
  • Revolution and the destruction of the Holy Roman Empire by Napoleonic armies, with German
  • Romantics and intellectuals developing an ethnic and linguistic definition of nationalism based
  • on the concept of the "cultural nation" (Kulturnation), while the German Confederation (Bund)
  • of 1815 reduced hundreds of fragmented sov ereign states to thirty -eight, serving as the
  • framework for nationalist aspirations. The Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 briefly indicated the
  • possibility of a democratic and united Germany, but the suppression of the democratic
  • movement and the defeat of liberals shifted the character of German unification from a liberal
  • democratic process to one shaped by conservative Prussian forces and the dynastic rivalry
  • between Prussia and Austria, culminating in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 which excluded
  • Austria from German affairs. Prussian Chancellor Otto von Bismarck's policy of "blood and
  • iron" decisively achieved unification through the defeat of France in 1871, compelling France
  • to relinquish Alsace as war indemnity, after which Wilhelm was proclaimed German Emperor
  • in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on January 18, 1871, formally uniting 25 German states
  • under Prussian leadership. Unlike France and Britain, the German nation state was not founded
  • on liberal democratic principles, as the German bourgeoisie was too weak to challenge the
  • conservative Junker landlords, leading instead to a "silent bourgeois revolution" that left
  • German political life significantly undemocratized despite the establishment of a national
  • parliament, the Reichstag.

questions.question: Examine the socio-economic scenario of Russia before the revolution of 1917. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the socio-economic scenario of Russia before the revolution of 1917. [An] / [CO1,
  • CO2, CO3,CO5] - Tsarist Russia was characterized by extreme social backwardness, with
  • about 70% of the population illiterate, no adequate public health or medical relief system,
  • widespread hunger among the majority, and a rigid social structure where a rich landed elit e
  • exploited the poor, while the Russian Orthodox Church provided ideological legitimacy to the
  • oppressive order and a corrupt bureaucracy showed no sympathy toward common people. The
  • peasantry, forming the vast majority of the population, experienced severe economic distress
  • that triggered major uprisings in Ukraine, the V olga areas, and Georgia in 1902, with over 3,000
  • peasant disturbances recorded by early 1905, leading to the formation of the All -Russian
  • Peasants' Union which demanded abolition of private property in land and the convening of a
  • constituent assembly. Industrial workers, though numbering only around 2 million, faced brutal
  • exploitation working 12 to 14 hours daily for low wages with no medical relief, weekly
  • holidays, or right to organize, as trade union formation was considered a crime, resulting in
  • mass strikes in 1902 and approximately 550 work stoppages by 1903, while the mutiny of
  • sailors on the battleship Potemkin in June 1905 reflected the spread of anger and
  • demoralization even into the armed forces. Politically, the Tsarist autocracy concentrated all
  • authority in the hands of the ruler while dismissing the representative Duma, a lienating
  • educated liberal Russians who increasingly supported the Union of Liberation movement, and
  • suppressing growing nationalist opposition movements among minority peoples in the Baltic
  • provinces, Ukraine, Poland, and Georgia, creating conditions of w idespread revolutionary
  • discontent across all sections of Russian society.

questions.question: Critically analyse dynamics occurred in the global political economy under the influence of Keynesian economics. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Critically analyse dynamics occurred in the global political economy under the influence
  • of Keynesian economics. [An] / [CO3] - Keynesian economics emerged as a direct response to
  • the catastrophic failures of laissez -faire capitalism exposed by the Great Depression of the
  • 1930s, with John Maynard Keynes arguing that aggregate demand was the primary driver of
  • economic growth and that governments must intervene through deficit spending, public works
  • programmes, and fiscal stimulus to restore employment, m ost notably demonstrated by
  • Roosevelt's New Deal which deployed massive state investment to pull America out of
  • depression. The Keynesian framework fundamentally transformed the relationship between the
  • state and the market by legitimising active government intervention, giving rise to the welfare
  • state across Western Europe and North America, where governments assumed responsibility
  • for social security, universal healthcare, public education, and unemployment insurance,
  • significantly reducing inequality an d social unrest in the post -war decades. The post -war
  • economic boom of 1945 –1973, often referred to as the "Golden Age of Capitalism,"
  • represented the triumphant application of Keynesian principles, as Western governments
  • maintained full employment policies, regulated financial markets, and coordinated
  • international economic stability through the Bretton Woods system, producing unprecedented
  • levels of sustained growth, rising wages, and expanding middle classes across the industrialised
  • world. However, the stagflation crisis of the 1970s exposed the limitations of Keynesian
  • demand management, triggering a neoliberal counter -revolution led by Thatcher and Reagan
  • that dismantled welfare provisions and deregulated markets, though the 2008 global financial
  • crisis dramatically renewed interest in state intervention, reaffirming the enduring relevance of
  • Keynesian economics in stabilising market economies.
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Discuss the role of Mao Zedong in the formation of the revolutionary China. / [CO1, CO2, CO5] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the role of Mao Zedong in the formation of the revolutionary China. [E] / [CO1,
  • CO2, CO5] - Mao Zedong emerged as a founding member of the Chinese Communist Party
  • (CCP) in 1921 and developed a distinctive form of Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions,
  • arguing that the peasantry rather than the urban proletariat would serve as the primary
  • revolutionary force, a theoretical innovation that fundamentally distinguished Chinese
  • communism from its Soviet counterpart. Following the betrayal of the Firs t United Front by
  • Chiang Kai-shek's Kuomintang in 1927, Mao led the famous Long March of 1934 –1935, a
  • gruelling 6,000-mile strategic retreat that established his undisputed leadership of the CCP and
  • transformed the communist movement into a disciplined revolutionary force rooted among the
  • rural peasant masses. Mao successfully led the CCP through the Second United Front against
  • Japanese occupation during World War II and the subsequent civil war against the Kuomintang,
  • culminating in the historic proclamation of the People's Republic of China on 1st October 1949,
  • establishing a communist state and ending a century of foreign humiliation and internal
  • fragmentation. As the paramount leader of the new republic, Mao pursued radical programmes
  • of land redistribut ion, nationalisation, and mass mobilisation through campaigns such as the
  • Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which whilst causing considerable
  • devastation, fundamentally reshaped Chinese society by dismantling feudal structures and
  • laying the ideological foundations of modern revolutionary China.
  • [10x2 = 20]
